headline: Agreed to a five-year limit for filing ethics complaints and forwarded confidentiality of complaints to Council.
summary: Members discussed a draft Code of Conduct for Council members and possible enforcement options, but made no decision on it. They agreed to a five-year filing limit for ethics complaints. They also agreed to send the Council a proposal to keep ethics complaints confidential until the Ethics Board reviews them.
decisions: Approved the March 30, 2026 meeting minutes with no dissenting votes.
Consented to a revision to the Citizen's Guide for Filing an Ethics Complaint, to be included in a report to the City Council.
Agreed to a five-year limit for filing ethics complaints, with an alternative allowing complaints during a term of office and for one year after it ends.
Referred to the City Council for its recommendation a concept to keep ethics complaints confidential until the Ethics Board reviews them.

decision_titles: Revision to Citizen's Guide for Filing an Ethics Complaint
Five-year limit for filing ethics complaints
Keeping ethics complaints confidential until Ethics Board review
plain_text:
City Council Rules Committee  
Draft Meeting Minutes 
September 28, 2026   
City Council Chambers 
37 Green Street 
3:00 PM  
 
1. Call to Order 
 
Councilor Kretovic called the meeting to order at 3:00 PM. 
 
2. Roll Call 
 
Present: Chair Jennifer Kretovic, Councilor Amanda Grady Sexton, Councilor Brent Todd 
 
Excused: Councilor Jeff  Foote, Councilor Judith Kurtz 
 
Also Present:  City Solicitor John Conforti, Deputy City Solicitor Danielle Sakowski 
 
3. Approval of Meeting Minutes 
 
• March 30, 2026 Draft Meeting Minutes 
 
Councilor Todd moved approval of the March 30, 2026 Meeting Minutes.  The motion 
was duly seconded by Councilor Amanda Grady Sexton and passed with no dissenting 
votes. 
 
4. Meeting overview  
 
Chair Kretovic reviewed the items for discussion. 
 
5. Items to be Considered Regarding the Amendment of Council Rules/Ethics 
Ordinance.  
 
• Code of Conduct.
2 
The Committee discussed the proposed Code of Conduct for City Council members. 
Members generally expressed support for the document as a useful framework 
establishing expectations for Council conduct, civility, communications, and interactions 
with City staff. It was noted that the Code of Conduct would provide an additional layer of 
guidance and a point of reference for Council members, particularly because there is 
currently limited guidance addressing certain types of conduct that may be inappropriate 
or discourteous but do not rise to the level of an ethics or Charter violation. Members 
discussed whether the Code of Conduct should be viewed primarily as an aspirational or 
“soft” policy establishing professional expectations, or whether it should include more 
specific enforcement provisions and sanctions. 
 
The Committee discussed the role of the City Solicitor and the relationship between the 
proposed Code of Conduct and the existing ethics framework. City Solicitor John Conforti 
explained that the Ethics Ordinance provides an enforcement mechanism administered by 
the City Council, while the Board of Ethics serves primarily in an advisory capacity. He 
noted that some conduct may be unbecoming or inconsistent with the expectations 
established in the Code of Conduct without necessarily constituting an ethics violation 
warranting a sanction. Members discussed whether conduct should be addressed as a 
matter of civility, professional expectations, or ethical obligations, and whether the Code 
of Conduct should expressly identify circumstances in which a sanction could be 
considered. City Solicitor Conforti noted that the Committee could either proceed with the 
Code of Conduct as a set of professional expectations or consider adding defined 
sanctions, however, additional sanctions would require corresponding procedures to 
ensure an appropriate process. 
 
Members also discussed the need for clarity regarding enforcement authority and process. 
Councilor Grady Sexton questioned the process for reprimanding a sitting Mayor, 
Councilor, or formally addressing the conduct of a Council member. It was noted that the 
current draft does not establish additional enforcement authority for the Council beyond 
existing provisions, although the draft could be expanded to provide additional options. 
The Committee discussed the possibility of using or adapting procedures contained in the 
existing ethics framework, including providing the Council with a range of options and 
establishing a process for consideration and action by the full Council. Members also 
discussed whether a Council vote, including a potential censure, could provide a separate 
mechanism for addressing violations of the Code of Conduct. Several members expressed 
concern that relying solely on the Mayor to address conduct could create limitations in 
circumstances involving conflicts, friendships, or other relationships, and suggested that 
the Council should have an independent mechanism for addressing concerns. 
 
The Committee further discussed specific provisions concerning communications and 
interactions with City staff, including the expectation that requests for staff work be
3 
directed through the City Manager and that competing demands on staff resources be 
respected. Members also discussed the need for a mechanism to address conduct that is 
perceived as targeting an individual, discourteous behavior, inaccurate statements, or other 
conduct that may warrant intervention but may not constitute an ethics violation. The 
Committee considered whether tools such as a point of order, a request for a conversation 
to address conduct, or other Council-directed actions could provide appropriate means of 
accountability. Members generally agreed that the proposed Code of Conduct provides a 
useful starting point and that further consideration should be given to the appropriate 
balance between aspirational standards and enforceable provisions, including what 
authority, sanctions, and procedural safeguards should accompany any additional 
enforcement mechanism. City Solicitor Conforti will draft proposed language outlining 
potential enforcement options and processes for the Committee’s review and further 
discussion. 
 
• Citizen Guide for Filing an Ethics Complaint. 
 
The Committee discussed revisions to the Citizen’s Guide for Filing an Ethics Complaint, 
including adding language addressing situations in which an individual falsely claims or 
represents that they are acting in an official capacity. Members noted that such conduct 
could potentially constitute a violation of the City Charter or an ethics violation. The 
Committee agreed that the Guide should not identify a specific Charter provision, as the 
circumstances may implicate different provisions depending on the facts of a particular 
complaint. 
 
The Committee also discussed the requirement that an ethics complaint be notarized and 
whether the current requirement could create an unnecessary barrier for individuals 
wishing to file a complaint, particularly those who are not residents or who are unable to 
appear in person. Members considered whether notarization requires the complainant to 
appear before the City Council and clarified that a complaint does not need to be presented 
directly to the Council. The Committee discussed whether the filing process could provide 
a practical means for a complainant to satisfy the notarization requirement while 
submitting a complaint remotely. 
 
City Solicitor Conforti reported that he had discussed the matter with Attorney Sullivan, 
Ethics Board Chair, and proposed making one revision to the language addressing the 
filing requirements. With the Committee’s consent, City Solicitor Conforti will make the 
proposed change and include the revised Citizen’s Guide in a report to the City Council.
4 
• Statutory Limits for Filing Ethics Complaints. 
 
The Committee held a brief discussion regarding establishing a statute of limitations for 
ethics complaints. City Solicitor Conforti noted that he had a conversation with Ethics 
Board Chair Attorney Sullivan who expressed support for a five-year limitation period, 
noting that this would align with the federal ethics complaint framework. Members noted 
that other jurisdictions, including some in New Hampshire, have adopted shorter or longer 
periods. The Committee discussed whether the limitation period should be tied to an 
individual’s time in office and generally favored a straightforward five-year period to 
provide sufficient time for a complaint to be brought while maintaining an appropriate 
level of timeliness. 
 
The Committee also discussed the application of the limitation period when an individual 
is no longer serving in office. City Solicitor Conforti explained that potential approaches 
could include an absolute five-year limitation period for matters before the Ethics Board 
or a limitation based on the individual’s term of office plus one year. Members noted that 
the latter approach would allow an additional year for an ethics complaint to be filed after 
an individual leaves office. The discussion included an example involving a former 
official who resigned following a controversy, with members noting that the additional 
one-year period would preserve an opportunity to bring a complaint and provide greater 
clarity regarding the timeframe for filing. 
 
The Committee agreed to a five-year limitation period, with an alternative provision 
allowing a complaint to be filed during an individual’s term of office and for one year 
following the end of the term. City Solicitor Conforti noted that the Ethics Ordinance will 
need to be amended, and the proposed changes will be included in the Council report with 
notice of a public hearing anticipated for November. 
 
• Should Ethic Complaints be Sealed/Non-Public under RSA 91-A with review by 
the Board of Ethics Before Release. 
 
The Committee discussed whether ethics complaints should be sealed or otherwise kept 
confidential until they have been reviewed by the Board of Ethics. City Solicitor Conforti 
reported that the Chair of the Ethics Board Attorney Sullivan had expressed concerns 
about fully sealing complaints. Based on his experience, there was concern that a process 
perceived as concealing complaints could lead to speculation or exacerbate public 
concerns if the public believed matters were being hidden. The Committee also discussed 
the requirements of RSA 91-A and the expectation that members of public bodies have a 
reduced expectation of privacy. City Solicitor Conforti noted that the Committee could 
ultimately determine the appropriate balance between transparency and protection from 
unwarranted reputational harm.
5 
 
Members expressed concerns about the potential impact of ethics complaints on 
individuals who are not the subject of the complaint, including volunteers serving on City 
boards and commissions. The Committee discussed the possibility of redacting names and 
other information that is ancillary or unrelated to the substance of a complaint. City 
Solicitor Conforti explained that RSA 91-A would permit appropriate redactions where 
warranted and distinguished this approach from automatically sealing an entire complaint 
before it has been reviewed. Members also expressed concern that the ethics complaint 
process could be used to cause reputational harm or otherwise be “weaponized,” 
potentially discouraging individuals from volunteering or serving in public office. It was 
noted that, under the current process, complaints are initially received by the City Clerk 
and forwarded to the Ethics Board, the accused subject of the complaint, and the 
Solicitor’s Office, and that complainants or others may independently provide complaints 
to the media. 
 
The Committee discussed a potential process under which an ethics complaint would 
initially be treated as confidential and reviewed by the Ethics Board before becoming 
subject to public inspection. City Solicitor Conforti explained that the Board could review 
the complaint, consider whether it alleges conduct warranting further action, and 
determine whether the complaint should remain confidential, be partially disclosed with 
appropriate redactions, or be opened to public inspection. He noted that the process would 
require the Board to conduct a balancing analysis, including consideration of potential 
reputational harm and the requirements of RSA 91-A. Members discussed whether the 
term “confidential” would be preferable to “sealed,” with City Solicitor Conforti noting 
that, functionally, both concepts would prevent public disclosure during the initial review, 
while “sealed” may imply a greater degree of authority or permanence. 
 
The Committee also discussed the importance of ensuring that the process does not 
prevent legitimate matters from being reviewed publicly when appropriate. City Solicitor 
Conforti noted that complaints would need to be reviewed by the Ethics Board before a 
determination could be made regarding confidentiality or disclosure, and that complaints 
that do not allege a matter warranting action could potentially be addressed without 
proceeding to a public hearing. Members agreed that the process should provide 
protections against complaints being used for improper purposes while preserving 
appropriate transparency and public accountability. The Committee reached consensus to 
forward the matter to the City Council for its recommendation, with the concept that ethics 
complaints would remain confidential until the Ethics Board has reviewed the complaint 
and determined the appropriate level of disclosure. City Solicitor Conforti will proceed 
with language using the concept of confidentiality rather than sealing as the basis for 
further consideration.
6 
6. Other Business 
 
7. Scheduling of Next Meeting 
 
The Committee agreed to schedule a follow up meeting.  Chair Kretovic will work with 
the City Clerk’s Office to schedule the next meeting, possibly October 26, 2026 at 3:30 
PM. 
 
8. Adjournment 
 
At 4:30 PM, there being no additional business to discuss, Councilor Grady Sexton 
moved to adjourn.  The motion was duly seconded by Councilor Todd, and passed with 
no dissenting votes. 
 
A true copy; I attest: 
 
Deborah Tuite 
Deputy City Clerk 
 
 
This meeting is open to the public although there is no public input or testimony.
